# Proteoforms and drug targeting

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/12-proteoforms-drugs.yml` and not yet reviewed by a
second reader.
:::

A drug binds a molecule with a particular shape, and
@sec-what-changes showed that one gene's isoforms can differ at exactly the
surfaces a drug would touch. If a gene makes several proteins, the practical
question is which one is the target, and whether anything can be aimed at that
one alone.

The vocabulary shifts from RNA to protein here. A transcript isoform
is an RNA molecule, while a proteoform is a distinct protein form from one gene,
and it absorbs differences this book has treated separately: those from
splicing, those from genetic variation, and those added after translation.

## What can be measured {#sec-measuring}

The gap between ambition and measurement is the largest in this book, and two
numbers set its size.

A single cell is estimated to carry upwards of a million different protein
forms, built from about 20,000 coding genes [@proteoformmedicine2026]. A single
intact-molecule study reports thousands of protein forms from a cell lysate
[@xu2024topdown]. The estimate counts in millions and the measurement in
thousands.

![Three quantities on one logarithmic axis. The gap between what is estimated to
exist and what one experiment reports is what limits isoform-level drug
discovery. The measured quantity is drawn as a band because the source says only
"thousands".](../figures/proteoform-scale.svg){#fig-proteoform-scale width=100%}

Two styles of mass spectrometry divide the problem. Reading fragments of a
protein gives information about regions of it, while reading the intact molecule
reports which combination of features one molecule actually carries
[@xu2024topdown]. Only the second can confirm that two differences sit on
the same protein.

The specific obstacle is abundance rather than principle. The peptide that
distinguishes one isoform from another is usually the scarce one, so isoforms go
unrecorded for want of signal [@korchak2024isprm]. @sec-is-it-translated showed
the same effect from the other side: detection tracked how well a gene was
covered.

Long reads from the same sample predict which isoform-specific peptides ought to
exist, and the instrument is then pointed at those [@korchak2024isprm]. It
works, raising isoform detectability 3.6-fold over the untargeted approach and
finding five isoforms that no annotation listed [@korchak2024isprm].

It confirmed protein for 54 resolved isoforms across 43 of 55 genes, and
required a synthetic standard for each of 192 peptides it hoped to find
[@korchak2024isprm]. This is not yet a survey method.

The block on drug discovery has been stated directly. A candidate
cannot be prioritised when it is unknown whether the splicing event yields a
protein, what that protein's structure is, and what it does
[@shaw2022multiomics]. Three therapeutic routes are already in use against
splicing events, which are immunotherapy, oligonucleotides and small molecules
[@shaw2022multiomics]. @sec-cancer-therapeutics and @sec-sma cover
examples of the second and third.

## A drug that targets one isoform {#sec-isoform-selective}

Claudin-18 settles the question of whether isoform-selective therapy is
possible, because it already exists in the clinic.

The gene makes two forms that differ only at the front of the protein, and the
difference traces to which first exon it uses. One belongs to stomach, the other
to lung [@katoh2026cldn18]. This is the alternative-promoter mechanism of
@sec-what-changes, arriving as a drug target.

![Two first exons, two proteins differing only at one end, and an antibody that
binds the loop present in one of
them.](../figures/cldn18-isoform-target.svg){#fig-cldn18 width=100%}

A monoclonal antibody against the stomach form, given with chemotherapy, holds
approval in the United States for gastric and gastro-oesophageal junction cancer
[@katoh2026cldn18]. Avoiding the other isoform was the design goal rather than a
side benefit, because the lung form is present in healthy lung and binding it
would do pulmonary harm [@katoh2026cldn18].

The general principle is stated in the same review. The point of targeting an
isoform rather than a gene is to leave the gene's other products alone
[@katoh2026cldn18]. That is the therapeutic argument for everything in this
book, and here it has a licensed drug attached to it.

The companion target in that review is one this book has already met. FGFR2b is
the epithelial form of a receptor whose IIIb and IIIc exons decide which growth
factors it answers to, described in @sec-fgfr. Both it and claudin-18 have
first-generation antibodies against them [@katoh2026cldn18].

How many patients the approach applies to depends on which antibody is used to
ask, and the clinical cut-offs differ between trials [@katoh2026cldn18].
Resistance is also expected to arrive by the mechanism that created the target,
with the tumour switching to an isoform that no longer carries the epitope
[@katoh2026cldn18].

::: {.callout-important}
## This narrows a verdict given earlier

@sec-cancer-therapeutics concludes that the isoform-level view of cancer has
changed what counts as a driver but not yet what counts as a treatment. That
holds for splicing-modulator drugs, which is the evidence it was drawn from. It
does not hold as a general statement. An approved first-line therapy already
depends on a distinction between two isoforms of one gene.
:::

## When the tumour changes isoform {#sec-resistance}

The resistance mechanism anticipated for claudin-18 has already been observed
elsewhere, which is the strongest reason to take it seriously.

HER2 is among the most studied targets in oncology. Reading its transcripts at
full length raised its protein-coding isoform count from 13 to 90
[@guardia2025her2]. Much of that diversity is invisible to the assays used in
the clinic, and went unrecognised until this survey of primary tumours
[@guardia2025her2]. Even the two HER2 variants that were already well known
turned out to be families: nine isoforms lacking exon 16 were found, of which
only 1 appeared in the reference annotation [@guardia2025her2].

The functional result is the one that matters, and it comes from cell cultures
rather than from treated patients. Lines made resistant to the antibody and to
antibody-drug conjugates came to favour forms of the receptor that no longer
carry the stretch the antibody grips [@guardia2025her2], so the target changed
shape.

The same lesson came first from cell therapy.
Relapse after CD19-directed treatment has been
attributed to the tumour switching which isoform of the target it makes
[@barnkob2022carisoform]. Auditing the antigens proposed for solid tumours
suggested the problem is general rather than specific to that one target
[@barnkob2022carisoform].

Those authors turned it into a selection rule, which is to aim at the isoforms a
tumour gains rather than at the ones it can afford to lose
[@barnkob2022carisoform].

Reviewed across antibody therapy as a whole, the same mechanism recurs on many
of the field's principal targets [@choi2025asresistance]. One recurring trick is
to make the target soluble, so it leaves the cell surface and absorbs the drug
or the immune signal while the cell goes unharmed [@choi2025asresistance]. The
death receptor FAS is a worked example: skipping one exon removes the membrane
anchor, and the soluble protein that results blocks the signal that would have
killed the cell [@choi2025asresistance].

This reframes @sec-drug-targets, where AR-V7 was presented as a target that
therapy creates. Isoform switching under drug pressure looks like the general
form of that behaviour rather than a peculiarity of the androgen receptor.

## Modalities being built {#sec-modalities}

If a target is an isoform, the binding reagent has to discriminate at that
resolution. Two approaches are being developed, and both run into the same
circular problem.

Single-domain antibodies keep full binding capacity at one-tenth the size of a
conventional antibody [@vanfossen2025nanobodies]. The property that matters here
is discrimination rather than affinity, since they can distinguish shapes of the
same protein that differ only slightly [@vanfossen2025nanobodies]. RPS24 showed
in @sec-rps24 that reagents of this selectivity can be made, for a difference of
three residues.

Raising a reagent against one protein form requires having that form in quantity
and purity first [@vanfossen2025nanobodies], so measurement and reagent
development are each waiting on the other.

Targeted degradation inherits the same blind spot in a more dangerous form. A
degrader designed against a protein does not distinguish that protein's forms,
so it may remove the harmless one and leave the harmful one to take over,
selecting for resistance [@cui2026proteoformdegradation]. Stated the other way
round, a drug aimed at a gene's canonical product may work against some of that
gene's protein forms and not others, so the result is adverse effects or a
failure to achieve what was expected [@cui2026proteoformdegradation].

A proteoform-blind drug need not fail outright to be failing part of the time.

## Proteoform medicine as a programme {#sec-programme}

The position now being argued is that protein forms sit between genotype and
phenotype rather than alongside them [@proteoformmedicine2026]. On that account
they are the layer at which disease mechanism and drug action actually operate.

Two technologies are named as making the programme feasible, and one of them is
the long-read sequencing of @sec-three-axes [@proteoformmedicine2026]. The claim
is framed as a dependency rather than an aspiration. Treatment at this
resolution requires measurement at this resolution [@proteoformmedicine2026].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What this book can and cannot say about that review

The review is in this corpus as an abstract only, so only its abstract-level
statements are cited here. Its account of the network biology, its treatment of
specific diseases, and any figure in it have not been read. Readers who want the
argument in full should go to the paper rather than to this section.
:::

## Where this leaves the argument

The position has three parts that do not resolve into one verdict.

Isoform-selective therapy already works in the clinic. An approved drug draws
its selectivity from which first exon a gene uses, and the design deliberately
spared the other isoform to avoid harming healthy tissue.

Isoform-blind therapy fails in a characteristic way. Cells escape by switching
to a form the drug cannot see, shown in culture for HER2, inferred from relapse
after CD19-directed treatment, and reviewed across antibody therapy. A target
defined at gene level carries that failure mode built in.

The measurement is also not yet adequate to the ambition. Confirming that a
particular protein form is present in a particular tissue, in enough copies,
with its epitope intact, remains a targeted experiment rather than a survey.
Until that changes, isoform-level drug discovery will proceed one gene at a
time, which is roughly where @sec-rps24 found it.
